questions.qtext:
Let $\Sigma = \{0,1\}$ be a binary alphabet. Consider the language $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$ consisting of all strings whose every prefix has at least as many $0$'s as $1$'s. Formally, for a string $w = w_1w_2w_3 \ldots w_n \in \Sigma^*$, $w \in L$ if and only if for every $k \in \{1,2,\ldots,n\}$, the prefix $w_1w_2 \ldots w_k$ contains at least as many $0$'s as $1$'s.

Which of the following options is true regarding the language $L$?

options.text: $L$ is not a context free language.
$L$ is a language of balanced parentheses.

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 1)
Option $\text{A}.$ FALSE
While reading strings of $L$, left to right, at no point should $\text{1's}$ exceed $\text{0's}$.
We can construct $\text{DPDA}$ for $L$.
So, $L$ is $\text{DCFL}$. And $\text{CFL}$ too.

Option $\text{B}.$ FALSE
Language of balanced parantheses requires string to have an equal number of $\text{0's}$ and $\text{1's}$
But $L$ also contains strings of unequal number of $\text{0's}$ and $\text{1's}$.
For e.g. $00011 \in L$

Option $\text{C}$. TRUE
$L$ is non-regular. In particular:
$S = \{0^n \mid n \ge 1 \}$ is an infinite distinguishing set for the language, because if we pick two distinct strings $0^p$ and $0^k$ ($p>k$) arbitrarily from $S$, we can append $0^p$ to distinguish them.
$0^p1^p \in L$ and $0^k1^p \notin L$ since $p>k$.

Option $\text{D}$. FALSE
$M = \{w \in {0,1}^* \mid |w|_0 \ge |w|_1\}$ is not same as $L$ because $010 \notin L$ but it is in $M$

Correct Answer: $\text{C}$
